Photograph: LegoCamera/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen It is the first time Incheon has topped the international passenger rankings since opening in 2001. Photograph: LegoCamera/Shutterstock Air transport South Korean airport becomes busiest in world for global traffic amid Iran war Incheon airport had 38.39m international passengers in first half of 2026, as traffic diverted from Middle East hubs Raphael Rashid in Seoul Thu 13 Aug 2026 05.45 EDT Last modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 06.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google South Korea’s Incheon airport has become the world’s busiest airport for international passengers, in part owing to disruption in the Middle East caused by the Iran war. The airport, South Korea’s main gateway, about 30 miles (48km) west of Seoul, handled 38.39 million international passengers in the first half of 2026, according to preliminary figures compiled by the Airports Council International (ACI), the global trade body for airports. Heathrow in the UK was second, with 37.79 million, followed by Changi airport in Singapore with 34.53 million. It is the first time Incheon has topped the international passenger rankings since opening in 2001. The airport was 10th in the world in 2002, rising to fifth in 2018 and third in 2024 and 2025. Part of the increase was attributed to disruption caused by the US-Iran conflict , which weakened the role of Middle Eastern hubs such as Dubai and diverted some transfer traffic to alternative routes through east Asia, Incheon International Airport Corporation (IIAC) was quoted as saying by the Yonhap news agency. Heathrow says need for expansion clear as it loses title of Europe’s busiest airport Read more Incheon’s international passenger traffic was up 6.3% year on year overall, with rising numbers of foreign visitors also contributing to the increase. Foreigners accounted for 39.3% of Incheon’s passengers in the first half of the year, up from 35.2% for the whole of 2025. The proportion reached a record 44.4% in the second quarter, with IIAC attributing the increase largely to growing numbers of visitors from China and Japan, according to local media. Heathrow, in west London, recorded 40 million passengers in total in the first half of the year, including both domestic and international travellers, its busiest first half on record. Passenger traffic to Asia-Pacific rose 7.9%, while capacity to the Middle East reportedly fell 16.5% owing to the regional conflict. Earlier this week Istanbul overtook Heathrow as Europe’s busiest airport by total passenger numbers. Figures published on Tuesday showed 7.9 million passengers passed through Heathrow’s terminals in July, compared with Istanbul’s 8.15 million. Incheon has also expanded its role as an international hub. It serves 101 airlines flying to 183 cities, including 158 international passenger destinations. A four-phase expansion completed in late 2024 increased the airport’s annual capacity to 106 million passengers. Kim Beom-ho, the acting president of IIAC, said the ranking reflected “the support of the government, the public’s encouragement and the hard work of everyone stationed at the airport”. South Korea also lays claim to the world’s busiest air route . The domestic corridor between Gimpo airport and Jeju island had 14.4 million seats scheduled in 2025, according to the aviation data provider OAG, more than any other route in the world. https://www.politico.eu/article/south-ko.text: South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said Wednesday that Seoul received no warning of Donald Trump’s plan to slash joint military exercises, a move the U.S. president announced publicly and linked to South Korea’s refusal to help with his war in Iran. “Neither our government nor U.S. officials knew what President Trump wrote on his Truth Social,” Cho told the National Assembly’s foreign affairs committee. “We were not notified in advance.” Trump ordered Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Sunday to “substantially reduce” the annual exercises, calling them costly and “totally inappropriate and hostile” toward North Korea. He tied the move to Seoul’s refusal to assist his effort to strip Iran of its nuclear capabilities and highlighted his “very good relationship” with Pyongyang's ruler Kim Jong Un. Advertisement Advertisement Cho said Trump’s announcement caught Seoul by surprise, but added the eventual changes to the drills were being worked out jointly. Defense Minister Ahn Gyu-back was in “close consultations” with Washington, he said. “Since our defense minister was involved in the discussions, I do not think it amounts to a unilateral notification.” He also warned that the smaller drills should not delay the transfer of wartime operational control, or OPCON, to Seoul — a longtime plan that would put a South Korean general in command of the combined U.S.-South Korean forces during a conflict. The drills have anchored the U.S.-South Korean alliance for more than 70 years , born from the aftermath of the Korean War, which ended in 1953 with an armistice agreement but no peace treaty. North Korea, which routinely condemns the drills as rehearsals for an invasion, launched another round of ballistic missile tests last week after this year’s exercises were announced. The rollback is already taking effect. South Korea said Wednesday that this year’s exercise will end on Aug. 21 rather than Aug. 27 after a U.S. request, cutting six days from the schedule.

Photograph: House of Commons View image in fullscreen Andy Burnham promised to bring optimism and ‘substantial change’ during his term. Photograph: House of Commons Andy Burnham Burnham blames Brexit and Thatcher for ‘wrong turns’ in first Commons speech as PM The prime minister said Britain needed to be brutally honest about the mistakes of the last 40 years of UK politics Pippa Crerar and Jessica Elgot Tue 1 Sep 2026 14.52 EDT Last modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 16.31 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Andy Burnham has blamed Brexit and Margaret Thatcher for a decade of low growth in the UK, arguing that Britain needs to be brutally honest about having taken “a series of wrong turns” in the last 40 years. In his first Commons appearance since he took over as prime minister about six weeks ago, Burnham told MPs he wanted to build a new sense of optimism so “we can make this next decade better than the last”. The British people wanted “much more substantial change” on the big issues facing the country, he said. “That is what I will bring. Britain is not where any of us would wish it to be. Things are not working as they should.” The UK economy has taken a 6% hit from the effects of Brexit , according to economists’ analysis of internal Bank of England data on thousands of British companies since the referendum a decade ago. More public control is the way to grow UK economy, Burnham to tell MPs Read more Shortly before Burnham’s Commons address, Keir Starmer, his predecessor, announced he would stand down as an MP , saying he wanted to focus on international affairs, triggering a tricky first byelection test for Burnham in a seat where the Greens fancy their chances. The cabinet was told on Tuesday that the government will have three key priorities: cutting costs of essentials like childcare and mortgages; the regeneration of communities; and greater public control of water, housing and energy. Burnham’s deputy, Louise Haigh, will lead task forces on each of those issues, the Guardian understands. He told his ministers they must be “relentless” in fulfilling his priorities. His plans are set against a tough economic backdrop . The chancellor’s headroom against Labour’s fiscal rules could be halved at his first budget if the current global bond sell-off persists, and economists warn mortgage rates could go up this autumn. In his Commons statement, the prime minister also: Hinted that he would commit to spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, saying he had appointed John Healey as his chancellor “precisely because” of his position on military spending . Signalled he is open to renationalising the water industry – saying he is looking at “all possible solutions”, as the sector is a “leaking monument” to the failures of privatisation. Opened the door to looking again at electoral reform in Labour’s next manifesto. “I do believe there needs to be a mandate to make that change. There are different views in this house, but I believe we will need to get a consensus at the next election. And if there is that consensus, then a change can be made in the next parliament.” Announced he would attend the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey and continue pursuing green energy – but that he would be “pragmatic” on supply, amid expectations he will approve the Jackdaw gasfield. “The mistake is saying it’s got to be one or the other for political purposes. The truth is, it’s going to have to be both.” Flanked by Healey and Haigh, Burnham suggested to MPs the Brexit vote had been a response to “a series of wrong turns” made by Britain in the 1980s onwards, that were then compounded by leaving the EU. The prime minister, whose Makerfield constituency voted for Brexit, has previously argued it would be a mistake to rerun the referendum – but has said that he wants the UK to rejoin in his lifetime. He suggested the next UK-EU reset summit could take place in November. Tax promises, defence targets and Iran: Andy Burnham’s budget headaches Read more “Political power was centralised, economic power privatised, the country de-industrialised. Austerity followed, hollowing out councils and depriving them of the agency to act to reverse any of this,” he said during a three-hour stint in the Commons. “And then Brexit compounded the damage, ushering in a decade of low growth and stalled regeneration. Change begins with honesty … Unless we are blunt about what went wrong, we won’t turn things around. “Far from taking back control, the combination of these policies took control out of the hands of communities up and down Britain for 40 years. Too many places have been drifting.” He added: “The government I lead will be relentless in giving people and places what they were promised 10 years ago: ownership and control, and from that control over their destiny comes change and growth.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines UK Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Kemi Badenoch accused Burnham of wanting to take the UK ‘back to the 1970s’. Photograph: House of Commons The Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, accused the prime minister of “living in the past” over his attacks on Thatcher – who was in power from 1979 to 1990 – and four decades of neoliberalism. “The year is 2026 but the prime minister said everything has gone wrong since the 1980s, still complaining about Margaret Thatcher. He is talking about a woman who became prime minister before I was born. He is living in the past and he wants to take us back to the 1970s.” In the statement, Burnham paid tribute to Starmer, saying he had created a platform for Britain to be fixed, “and we will use it well”. Just hours earlier, his predecessor announced he would be standing down as MP for Holborn and St Pancras, despite saying in July he planned to stay on until the next election. “It has been a huge honour and privilege to represent the best constituency in the country,” he said. “I will now focus on other things and that will be international affairs, including defence, security, trade and technology in a fast-changing world.” Starmer’s seat, long seen as a safe Labour hold, is likely to be targeted by the Greens, potentially for party leader Zack Polanski, who is a London Assembly member. “Zack has always made it clear he would like to be a London MP. London has been his home for over 20 years,” a Green spokesperson said. Just as the Makerfield byelection was seen as a proof of concept for whether Burnham could beat Reform, so the north London seat will test his progressive credentials. Labour will choose its candidate to replace Starmer next Wednesday under an accelerated selection timetable. Burnham’s first taskforce will be charged with finding bold solutions to tackling “everyday rip-offs”. The cost of living taskforce will look at parking charges, subscription traps and cowboy builders, as well as long-term fixed pressures like mortgages, food costs and childcare. The second will assess the affordability and practicalities of the state taking over failing essential services. Burnham believes that greater state control of essential services is the surest way to economic growth, avoiding the potential for ineffective profiteering by privatised services. Government sources said that Haigh, the first secretary of state, wanted to look beyond sectors such as transport and explore serious opportunities for greater state control in areas like energy and housing – if it would bring down ordinary people’s costs. The third taskforce will explore more radical ideas to revive crumbling high streets and impoverished districts, such as potential legislative options on houses in multiple occupation, as well as devolving powers to mayors and councils to help them regenerate local high streets. Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/AP View image in fullscreen Donald Trump’s decision to pause sanctions against Russia for its war against Ukraine has been criticised by Republicans and Democrats. Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Russia Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Trump’s sanctions waiver is a ‘60-day pause’ to analyse economic impact, says Rubio Ukraine’s Zelenskyy expects Trump to lift more sanctions against Russia. What we know on day 1,698 Guardian staff and agencies Sat 17 Oct 2026 21.07 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google US secretary of state Marco Rubio has said that US President Donald Trump’s waiver of sweeping sanctions and tariffs on Russia would be a 60-day pause to “analyse” their impact on the global economy. Rubio said also no one at the White House ordered the slow down of the speed of Ukraine’s access to Starlink to prevent it from being used on drones flying faster than 100mph, referring to Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite internet network. “The president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy,” Rubio said, noting that the economic restrictions involved a number of countries, not just Russia. Pointing to high energy prices and the Iran war, “we need that period of time to sort of study all this and figure out what the right combination is,” he said. Trump’s abrupt decision to waive sanctions on Russia days before they were to take effect drew outrage Saturday from members of Congress , which had overwhelmingly passed the legislation. Republican Senator Rick Scott said it was clear Russia was the aggressor, and said the US had “to do everything we can to put economic pressure on Russia”. On social media, fellow Republican Thom Tillis described the move as “beyond irresponsible” and a capitulation “to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine”. The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy expects the Trump administration to lift more sanctions against Russia in the future and has called for Europe to establish its own negotiations with Moscow as the US has sought better ties and business deals with the Kremlin. “Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue, and I believe that the ‘diesel deal’ is the first step,” said Zelenskyy on Saturday. “Unfortunately, it seems to me that this cannot stop Putin; on the contrary, he feels joy and happiness that he has such support.” Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s lead negotiator, Rustem Umerov, had met Friday with US presidential envoy Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law . Zelenskyy said the US was working to arrange a three-way meeting involving him, Trump and Putin, potentially in the Middle East, Europe or the US. Russian air defence ⁠units intercepted and destroyed nearly ⁠200 Ukrainian ⁠drones ​headed for Moscow on Saturday, ⁠Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Telegram. Sobyanin, ⁠in a long ​series ‌of ‌online posts, noted ‌that 195 drones had been destroyed since midnight, with emergency crews examining debris on ‌the ground. Russia’s civil aviation authority, ​Rosaviatsia, said two Moscow airports – Domodedovo and Vnukovo – had ⁠suspended flight operations. Romania said Saturday it shot down two Russian drones over the Black Sea, the latest in a spate of incidents believed to be spillover from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine . Ships have been attacked in recent days by drones in the Black Sea off the coast of Romania and Bulgaria. NEW YORK, NY .- This fall, The Metropolitan Museum of Art presents The Parade (ca. 1950), a work comprised of 63 drawings by Polish-born artist Si Lewen (1918–2016). On view from October 1, 2026, through January 5, 2027, the presentation is the first public exhibition of the work since the Museum acquired it in 2024. Created in the years following World War II, the epic sequence of charcoal, pencil, and ink drawings is informed by Lewen's extraordinary life. Born in Poland to Jewish parents and raised in Germany, Lewen fled Nazi persecution with his family in 1933, spending a brief period in France before immigrating to the United States. During World War II, he served in the U.S. Army as one of the Ritchie Boys, a specialized unit of German-speaking soldiers. After seeing action in Normandy, he was present at Buchenwald concentration camp shortly after its liberation in 1945, experiences that shaped The Parade into a powerful meditation on war, memory, and the human condition. BERGAMO .- GAMeC—Galleria d’Arte Moderna e Contemporanea di Bergamo presents 1000 Tears, the first solo exhibition by artist Selma Selman in an Italian institution. Among the most significant voices on the international art scene, Selman—born in 1991 in Bihać, Bosnia and Herzegovina—has built much of her research around the history of her family and community. Her practice investigates systems of power and the ways in which they shape value, visibility, memory, and belonging. Moving across painting, film, performance, and research-based forms, she examines how social, economic, political, and cultural structures determine whose bodies, histories, labor, and experiences are recognized, represented, or erased. The core of the project is a photograph taken during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, featuring the artist as a child alongside members of her family. EDINBURGH .- A major new exhibition at the National Museum of Scotland will challenge perceptions of one of Scotland's most renowned monarchs. Mary, Queen of Scots: Renaissance and Resistance (12 Jun – 14 Nov 2027) will bring together around 100 loans from across Europe, some never seen before in Scotland. The exhibition will present a vibrant Renaissance monarch on a European stage and a Scottish queen fiercely resisting those who conspired to take her crown, and ultimately, her life. In 1561 the widowed teenager Mary, Queen of Scots returned from France to a Scotland riven by the Protestant Reformation. This revolution had seismic consequences for Mary and for the Scottish people as the iconoclastic kirk’s tentacles extended throughout daily life and Protestantism became a key marker of Scottish nationhood. BRUSSELS .- Bozar presents the first retrospective exhibition dedicated to Jean Brusselmans (Brussels, 1884 – Dilbeek, 1953) since 1980. Featuring 120 paintings, drawings and engravings – including masterpieces from major museum collections as well as little known gems – Bozar celebrates one of the most distinctive painters of the Belgian avant-garde. From the beginning of the 20th century, Brusselmans developed a unique oeuvre, unbound by artistic trends yet firmly rooted in the tradition of painting. Through 120 works and dialogues with his contemporaries – such as Léger, Mondrian, Morandi, Wouters and Permeke -, the exhibition delves into the world of this singular painter, between abstraction and figuration. Brusselmans’s view of the world was as modest as it was profound. NEW YORK, NY .- In 1936, at the outset of the Spanish Civil War, Esteban Vicente (Turégano, Segovia, 1903–Bridgehampton, New York, 2001) relocated to the United States, a country where he would live for the rest of his life. There, he forged a network of personal and professional relationships that led him to become a part of the American Abstract Expressionist movement, closely associating with its leading figures and earning the esteem of its most notable gallerists and critics. These influences were met with the background of a Spanish artist who, before his departure, had visited some of Europe's greatest art capitals, like Paris and London, embracing the most advanced art of his time. From all this emerged a singular body of work of rich significance to both American and Spanish art of the second half of the twentieth century. LONDON .- In Spring 2027, the Hayward Gallery will present the largest UK solo exhibition to date by the internationally-celebrated Chinese multimedia artist Cao Fei (b. 1978). Charting the development of a figure at the forefront of technological revolution in contemporary art, the survey will mark the UK debut of The Birth (2026) alongside her most seminal works, including Whose Utopia (2006), RMB City (2007–2011) and Asia One (2018). https://24.hu/kulfold/2026/11/21/zelensz.text: A Krími hidat előbb-utóbb megsemmisítik, és ezt Vlagyimir Putyin orosz elnöknek is meg kell értenie – jelentette ki Volodimir Zelenszkij ukrán elnök az NBC amerikai televíziónak pénteken adott interjújában. Zelenszkij szerint Ukrajnának joga van támadni a Krími hidat, amelyet Oroszország a félsziget 2014-es elfoglalása után épített, és amelyen jelentős mennyiségű fegyvert szállít a megszállt ukrán területekre. Az ukrán elnök hangsúlyozta, hogy országa nem fogadja el területeinek orosz megszállását, és azt sem, hogy Moszkva katonai célokra használja ezeket a területeket. Az ukrán elnök emlékeztetett arra, hogy az orosz hadsereg évek óta támadja Ukrajna infrastruktúráját. Mint mondta, az orosz erők az idén az ukrán vasútvonalakat és hidakat is többször támadták. – fogalmazott, hozzátéve, hogy az orosz támadásokra a jövőben is válaszolni fognak. A Krím félszigetet az orosz szárazfölddel összekötő, 19 kilométer hosszú Krími híd Putyin egyik legfontosabb presztízsberuházása. A közúti és vasúti hídból álló átkelőt az Ukrajna elleni teljes körű orosz invázió kezdete óta a megszállt területeken harcoló orosz csapatok utánpótlására is használják. Az ukrán hadsereg ezen a héten háromszor támadta meg a hidat. A november 17-i csapás következtében a közúti híd egyik szakasza a tengerbe omlott, két nappal később pedig a vasúti pályát is találat érte. Az orosz hatóságok elismerték, hogy a híd súlyosan megrongálódott, helyreállításának időpontja egyelőre bizonytalan.

https://www.justsecurity.org/163937/earl.text: Early Edition: November 10, 2026 By Ammanuel Desta Published on November 10, 2026 Listen to Article Sign up to receive the Early Edition in your inbox here . A curated weekday guide to major news and developments over the last 24 hours. Here’s today’s news: IRAN WAR President Trump yesterday reiterated that a renewed military campaign against Iran is “quite unlikely,” and “doesn’t seem to be necessary.” Trump’s comments were made on social media and at an impromptu press conference, and he added that “we want a long-term solution.” Trump told Reuters that Qatar and Saudi Arabia were eager for a peaceful solution to the Iran conflict but that the United States was ready to resume military strikes if necessary. Barak Ravid reports for Axios ; Steve Holland reports for Reuters . Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani on social media yesterday described his talks with Trump and U.S. Vice President JD Vance about Iran as “positive.” The prime minister said he was “grateful for the positive discussions on reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region.” France’s foreign minister today said the Qatari prime minister will make an unscheduled stop at the G7 foreign ministers meeting in Paris, France. Tara Suter reports for The Hill ; John Irish reports for Reuters . IRAN WAR – OTHER DEVELOPMENTS France yesterday accused Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of being behind last month’s temperature-raising hack of French supermarket fridges and freezers. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the attack was “unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression,” and added that those responsible would be hit with sanctions. Iranian media outlets have dismissed the allegations as baseless, while France today summoned Iran’s ambassador. Ella Kipling and Joe Tidy report for BBC News ; John Irish reports for Reuters . Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand at the G7 meeting today said Canada reimposed sanctions on 11 Iranian entities for their contribution to Iran’s nuclear activities and ballistic missile program. Anand said the measures were intended to restrict Iran’s access to funding and sensitive technology linked to its nuclear and missile programs. Rishabh Jaiswal reports for Reuters . The United States yesterday evacuated U.S. aircraft from the U.K. Royal Air Force base in Mildenhall in the wake of a threat from Iran, sources told the Wall Street Journal . The sources said the precise nature of the threat to RAF Mildenhall remains under discussion among U.S. officials. Shelby Holliday and Alexander Ward report. RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR Russian and Ukrainian officials today met in Abu Dhabi for their first U.S.-brokered talks since Feb. 2026. U.S. Special Envoy Jared Kushner told delegates that recent contacts with both sides had “really identified, narrowed the gaps,” and that Trump was committed to achieving peace. Roula Rouhana reports for Reuters . The White House is “cautiously optimistic” about the peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi this week, U.S. officials told Axios . A U.S. official said the “relations we have built with [Russian President Vladimir] Putin will be instrumental in these negotiations,” while another U.S. official said U.S. Special Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner may travel to Ukraine and Russia to speak directly with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Putin. Barak Ravid reports. Russia believes the main thrust of U.S.-brokered peace talks on Ukraine should be seeking agreement on the main elements of a post-war security framework for Europe, a source in the Russian delegation told Reuters . The source said the Ukrainian settlement “is just one aspect of this wide-ranging discussion and is subordinate to the main objective – the creation of a comprehensive and indivisible security architecture for the entire continent.” Andrew Osborn reports. OTHER GLOBAL DEVELOPMENTS Poland’s Internal Security Agency today said two Ukrainian men suspected of espionage and sabotage on behalf of Russian intelligence services were arrested. The agency said “the suspects carried out tasks on behalf of Russian special services, which included, among other things, reconnoitring critical infrastructure and military facilities throughout the country.” Anna Koper reports for Reuters . The United Kingdom today said it would spend £90 million on drones, sensors, and AI systems to help the Royal Navy counter Russian undersea threats in the North Atlantic and protect critical infrastructure. Sarah Young reports for Reuters . Actor Russell Brand yesterday was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison in a U.K. court, after being convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault last Thursday. The judge described Brand as a “sexual predator” and criticized his “staggering arrogance.” Sima Kotecha and Steven McIntosh report for BBC News . Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar yesterday said Hungary has detained the brother of former prime minister Viktor Orban during its investigation of a people-smuggling case. Magyar said “three out of the ex-ministers of Orban are already in custody.” Anita Komuves reports for Reuters . The spokesperson for the U.N. Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker T ü rk, Thameen Al-Kheetan, today voiced alarm about Egyptian authorities’ widening assaults on press freedom and called for the immediate release of detained journalists. Al-Kheetan said “these alarming developments must end immediately, and journalists must be able to carry out their essential work free from intimidation and reprisals.” Emma Farge reports for Reuters . Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korean Leader Kim Jong Un, today expressed regret over comments by U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urging the two Koreas to ease tensions through dialogue following a landmine blast at the border last September. Kim Yo Jong said Guterres took a “prejudiced and irresponsible” attitude by echoing South Korea’s unilateral claim. Jack Kim reports for Reuters . Indonesian Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka today expressed his intention to resign during a meeting with President Prabowo Subianto, presidential spokesperson Prasetyo Hadi said. Hadi said the president didn’t decline the vice president’s request to resign. Stefanno Sulaiman, Ananda Teresia, and Stanley Widianto report for Reuters . Paraguayan public schoolteachers yesterday went on strike following the collapse of the major bank Ueno linked to former Paraguayan president Santiago Peña. President of the Federation of Paraguayan Educators Silvio Piris said that teachers are concerned over the fate of around $60 million in pension funds that had been deposited in Ueno. AP News reports. CLIMATE DEVELOPMENTS Brazil today will launch its road map to “transition away from fossil fuels” during the COP31 meeting in Turkey. The document is designed with different “levers” for countries to use to switch from coal, oil, and gas to renewable energies such as wind and solar. The Brazilian CEO of last year’s COP meeting Ana Toni told AP News that “what we hope to achieve with the road map is making a big problem, that is transitioning away, translating it into smaller actionable solutions.” Suzan Fraser, Sibi Arasu, and Seth Borenstein report. AI DEVELOPMENTS Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese today said the country plans to create an AI safety regulator in response to OpenAI’s breach of an Australian Health Department website in June. Albanese said the regulator would enforce legislated AI standards that would apply to all frontier AI companies that want to operate in Australia, and that financial penalties would apply, although the penalties are yet to be detailed. Rod McGuirk reports for AP News . Nvidia shareholders yesterday sued the company, alleging that CEO Jensen Huang’s failure to disclose his affair with Alice Huang artificially inflated share prices. The lawsuit also contends that the national security concerns raised by the allegations present a material risk to the company’s reputation and future business prospects. Andrew Atterbury reports for POLITICO . Trump yesterday said Jensen Huang told him that he was not aware that Alice Huang was an intelligence operative for China. Trump told reporters “I asked [Jensen] that question: ‘Did you have any idea that she was a spy?’” and “He said, ‘I had no idea that she was a spy,’ and I really believe him.” Trump also confirmed the FBI was looking into Jensen’s affair, but that “I think that [Jensen will] be in good shape.” Luke Broadwater and Maggie Haberman report for the New York Times ; Steve Holland, Courtney Rozen, Karen Freifeld, and David Shepardson report for Reuters . Microsoft has been pressing the Trump administration to halt plans to bar Chinese imports of a key component used in AI data centers, sources told Reuters . The White House is concerned that the use of Chinese optical transreceivers would allow China to steal data, install malware, or disrupt service at U.S. data centers. Alexandra Alper reports. U.S. MIDTERM DEVELOPMENTS Trump on social media yesterday appeared to go back on his acceptance of midterm election results and said “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest.” Trump further wrote “How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting ‘dumps’ were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote. It’s all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter!” Luke Broadwater and Zolan Kanno-Youngs report for the New York Times . Vance yesterday joked about a “devastating loss” last week while addressing veterans at an event in the capital. Vance said “there are a lot of people unfairly criticizing the leader of the team despite leading us to a great victory two years ago,” and joked that “there’s a conversation about whether the number two has what it takes to lead the team,” in reference to the Ohio State Buckeyes. Mallory Wilson reports for The Hill . U.S. FOREIGN AFFAIRS The United States today will spurn a U.N. meeting where its human rights record under Trump was due to be examined. The White House last year disengaged from the U.N. Human Rights Council, citing an anti-Israel bias, and it’s the second year in a row that it has skipped its own review. Emma Farge reports for Reuters . China wants any three-way summit between Trump, Putin, and Chinese President Xi Jinping to be a highly scripted affair, with each reading a prepared statement, sources told the Wall Street Journal . The sources said the Trump administration is pushing for a looser format that would allow more exchange among the three leaders, and the differences between the two sides raise doubts about whether the meeting will happen. Lingling Wei reports. U.S. oil company Exxon Mobil yesterday said it reached a non-binding preliminary deal with Venezuela to evaluate oil production opportunities in the country. Exxon in a statement said that “any future investment would require stable policies, clear regulations, strong investment protections, and competitive returns.” Rebecca F. Elliott reports for the New York Times . Derek Utley, co-founder of digital firm X Strategies, yesterday accused his co-founder and MAGA media guru Alex Bruesewitz of receiving gifts from foreign individuals in Qatar and Syria while also pursuing lucrative deals with other entities looking to unlock access to U.S. government officials. Bruesewitz is a top outside adviser to Trump and X Strategies still maintains the Trump War Room and Team Trump accounts on some social media platforms. The allegations were made in a court filing , after X Strategies in September sued Utley, alleging he embezzled and gambled away millions of dollars from the firm. Utley called the suit against him a “marketing ploy masquerading as a federal lawsuit” and denies the allegations. Jason Beeferman reports for POLITICO . U.S. IMMIGRATION DEVELOPMENTS Trump yesterday defended his administration’s immigration policy and said he was opposed to any immigration deal that would include “amnesty” for immigrants living in the United States illegally. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin also said that while he has been fielding calls from Democrats interested in working on immigration policy, he was opposed to any deal that would include amnesty. Rebecca Santana reports for AP News . U.S. DOMESTIC DEVELOPMENTS Karen Attiah yesterday announced she would not return to her job as a Washington Post opinion columnist even after an arbitrator ruled she was unjustly fired for statements following the killing of Charlie Kirk. Attiah said she would not return due to a lack of “guaranteed freedom and institutional support” within the Post newsroom. Attiah sued for wrongful termination after she was fired for writing that the United States “accepts and worships gun violence,” and posted a quote from Kirk in which he said a number of prominent Black women didn’t have the “brain processing power” to be taken seriously. Ryan J. Karlin reports for The Hill . Nonprofit organization Hispanic Scholarship Fund yesterday said the scholarships they provide for Hispanic students will be open to applicants of all races and ethnicities from Jan. 2027. The move is part of a settlement agreement in a lawsuit filed by the American Alliance for Equal Rights that claimed the awards were discriminatory. The HSF said it will not consider an applicant’s race or ethnicity but will instead offer the scholarships to students who “demonstrate a commitment” to the success of Hispanics in the United States. Madeleine Rubin reports for the New York Times . California voters rejected a one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ net worth, based on a final tally of results issued yesterday. During the run-up to the Nov. 3 election, the “no” side raised roughly 10 times as much as the “yes” side, with Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone spending more than $100 million into a political action committee working to defeat the measure. The “Yes on 40” campaign said the measure sought to protect healthcare for Californians and that they will put a tax back on the ballot in 2028 if patients are not protected. Sophie Austin reports for AP News . House Democrats are demanding that the Interior Department retains documents related to Trump’s construction projects around Washington D.C. after whistleblowers warned that key paperwork has already been destroyed before Democrats take power, congressional sources told CNN . The top Democrat in the House Natural Resources Committee today plans to issue letters to the Interior Department as well as other federal agencies and private companies, requesting that they “preserve all records and data responsive to oversight.” Sunlen Serfaty and Annie Grayer report. House Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) yesterday introduced eight articles of impeachment accusing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth of violating federal law and the Constitution, and abusing his authority. The articles accuse Hegseth of waging war without congressional authorization and continuing the military campaign after Congress voted to direct Trump to terminate the conflict or seek authorization to continue it, and of violating deadlines under the War Powers Resolution, which requires the withdrawal of U.S. forces from unauthorized hostilities after 60 days. The remaining charges accuse Hegseth of carrying out unlawful military strikes against suspected drug traffickers, unlawfully capturing Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, conducting unauthorized military operations in Yemen, disregarding laws intended to minimize civilian casualties, and abusing his power by retaliating against Sen. Mark Kelly (D-AZ) for protected speech. The vote must occur by tomorrow. Robert Jimison reports for the New York Times .
